citations.text: Lieberman, D. E. (2011). The Evolution of the Human Head. Harvard University Press.

en.general: The arrangement of parts that gives a system its properties and determines its function. In evolutionary anthropology: skeletal morphology encoding evolutionary history, kinship structures regulating cooperation, grammatical structures enabling communication, population genetic structure reflecting migration history, social hierarchy organizing primate groups.

oe:accessibleInstantiations.example: A human spine is built to hold the body upright — that structure makes walking on two legs possible.
DNA is built like a twisted ladder — the rungs of the ladder are the letters of the code that tells cells what to build.
A kinship system is a set of rules about who counts as family — that structure determines who helps whom and who can marry whom.

The regulatory structure of the FOXP2 gene — which enhancers control its expression, in which tissues, at which developmental stages — is what makes the human version of the gene produce different effects than the chimpanzee version.

3-5.classroomInstantiation: Learning about skeletal structure and its evolutionary implications; understanding that DNA has a structure (four-letter code) that determines what proteins get made; mapping the branching structure of a language family tree.
3-5.educatorBridgingNote: At 3–5, structure moves from the surface to the interior. Students discover that hidden organization — in bones, in DNA, in family trees — determines outcomes. The grammar of a language is a structure you use without seeing; a genome is a structure inside every cell. Help students appreciate that invisible structure is real and consequential.
3-5.studentFacingDescription: Things are organized on the inside in ways you can't always see — and that organization determines what they can do.

6-8.classroomInstantiation: Analyzing kinship structures as rules that organize who can marry whom and how resources flow; understanding population genetic structure as statistical patterns of allele frequency difference between groups; identifying grammatical structure in an unfamiliar language.
6-8.educatorBridgingNote: At 6–8, structure becomes genuinely abstract — students must accept that 'kinship structure' or 'population genetic structure' are real phenomena even though they cannot be directly observed. Use multiple representations to make abstract structure concrete: kinship diagrams, population structure bar charts, phylogenetic trees. Each is a representation of a structure that exists in social or biological reality.
6-8.studentFacingDescription: Some structures can't be seen at all — they are patterns of relationships that organize a system.

9-12.classroomInstantiation: Analyzing regulatory genomic architecture and how enhancer-promoter structure determines when and where genes are expressed; modeling how different kinship structures create different cooperation incentives; comparing the tree topology (branching structure) of genetic, linguistic, and cultural phylogenies.
9-12.educatorBridgingNote: At 9–12, structure becomes a formal object of analysis — something that can be represented mathematically, compared across systems, and used to generate predictions. The key sophistication is understanding that structure constrains possibility: a genome with a particular regulatory architecture can only produce certain phenotypes; a kinship system with particular rules can only generate certain cooperation patterns.
9-12.studentFacingDescription: The structure of a system can be formally specified and modeled — and different structures generate different behaviors and evolutionary dynamics.

K-2.classroomInstantiation: Comparing human and chimpanzee hands, feet, and spines; observing that a bird's beak shape matches what it eats; feeling the difference between flat teeth (grinding) and pointed teeth (tearing).
K-2.educatorBridgingNote: At K–2, structure is entirely physical and functional: this shape does this job. The key vocabulary is 'built for' — 'human hands are built for...' 'chimpanzee feet are built for...' This is the implicit foundation for adaptation, which debuts formally at 3–5. Do not yet name adaptation; let the idea live in the physical comparison.
K-2.studentFacingDescription: Things are built in a specific way — and that shape helps them do specific things.

extensions.oe:scopeNote: Structure bridges the visible and invisible: at K–2 it is physical form that can be touched and seen; by 9–12 it is abstract organizational schema that can only be inferred. The key insight across all grade bands is that structure is not arbitrary — it encodes history and determines function. A skull's shape encodes millions of years of selection; a kinship system encodes solutions to cooperation problems; a genome's regulatory architecture encodes developmental history.
